title: The 'Concorde Fallacy' Keeping You in Dead-End Projects
alt_title_1: One Question That Breaks the Sunk Cost Trap Instantly
alt_title_2: Why Smart People Pour Good Years After Bad Decisions
description_hook: Britain and France kept funding the supersonic Concorde long after it was clear it would never pay back its costs. This video shows how the Concorde Fallacy traps ambitious builders and the Zero-Base Question to escape it.

scenes.headline: Why High Achievers Stay Too Long
scenes.stat_label: AVERAGE DELAY BEFORE EXITING DEAD PATHS
bullets: Intelligent people rarely struggle to start hard things
They struggle to walk away once an investment stops paying
scenes.narration: Why do smart people stay in draining careers, dead-end side projects, and broken commitments for years after they clearly stop working?

scenes.headline: The 1976 Supersonic Money Pit
bullets: Concorde was never expected to repay its development costs
Both governments kept paying so past spending would not look wasted
scenes.narration: Biologists Richard Dawkins and Tamsin Carlisle named it the Concorde Fallacy in 1976, the year the supersonic jet entered service. Britain and France kept funding Concorde long after it was clear it would never pay back its costs.
scenes.source: Dawkins & Carlisle, 'Parental investment, mate desertion and a fallacy', Nature (1976)

scenes.headline: Throwing Future Margin After Past Pride
scenes.left_body: 'I already spent 3 years here -> I cannot walk away now'
scenes.right_body: Past costs are gone -> price only the next 12 months
scenes.narration: Your brain hates admitting a loss so intensely that it throws precious future years after unrecoverable past years. Past time and past money are gone forever.

scenes.headline: Ask the Zero-Base Entry Question
scenes.stat_subtext: Cut dead weight fast -> compound fresh upside
scenes.narration: Break the spell with the Zero-Base Question: knowing everything I know today, if I were not already inside this project or commitment right now, would I enter it from scratch?

scenes.headline: Walking Away Early Is Capital Allocation
scenes.stat_label: JUDGE EVERY COMMITMENT FROM TODAY FORWARD
bullets: Never pay future life energy to defend a past mistake
Audit your top 3 commitments every quarter from Day 0
scenes.narration: If the honest answer is no, walk away. That frees your time and money for something better.
scenes.source: Mind & Margin rule of thumb (advice, not a study)
